label: The Sphere Theorem
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 265 to 285, builds toward one of Riemannian geometry's landmark results. We will see how a purely metric pinching hypothesis on sectional curvature forces a complete simply connected manifold to be topologically a sphere, and assemble the comparison machinery that makes the conclusion possible.

label: Pinched Curvature
notes: The hypothesis is strict quarter pinching: sectional curvature lies in the half open interval one quarter to one. We normalize the upper bound to one so distances compare against the unit sphere. The strictness at one quarter is essential, since the closed condition admits other space forms like projective spaces.

label: Statement of the Theorem
notes: Here we state the topological sphere theorem precisely. A complete simply connected manifold whose sectional curvature is strictly quarter pinched is homeomorphic to the n-sphere. We stress homeomorphic, not diffeomorphic, since the smooth refinement required decades more work and exotic spheres complicate the differentiable picture.

label: Conjugate Points and Rauch
notes: Rauch comparison controls how fast geodesics spread according to curvature bounds. With curvature at most one, no conjugate point occurs before distance pi, so geodesics of length less than pi minimize against that obstruction. This conjugate point estimate is the first half of bounding the injectivity radius from below.

label: Injectivity Radius
notes: The injectivity radius is the largest radius on which the exponential map stays a diffeomorphism. It is governed by two competitors: the first conjugate point along a geodesic, and half the length of the shortest closed geodesic. Bounding it below is the geometric heart of the proof we now pursue.

label: Klingenberg's Lemma
notes: Klingenberg's lemma states that the injectivity radius equals the minimum of the conjugate radius and half the shortest closed geodesic length. Under quarter pinching the conjugate radius is at least pi, and a separate argument bounds the closed geodesic, yielding an injectivity radius of at least pi for the manifold.

label: The Diameter Bound
notes: Combining the lower curvature bound one quarter with Bonnet Myers gives a diameter at most two pi. Together with the injectivity radius at least pi, every point lies within reach of a single exponential chart from suitable centers. These two metric estimates frame the covering we will build from two balls.

label: Toponogov Comparison
notes: Toponogov's theorem compares geodesic triangles in our pinched manifold against model triangles on the sphere of curvature one quarter. Angles in our manifold are no smaller than the comparison angles. Berger applied this hinge comparison to control how far apart two maximally distant points sit and to align the two covering balls.

label: Two Geodesic Balls
notes: Pick a point p and a point q at maximal distance. The open balls of radius pi about p and about q are each diffeomorphic to a Euclidean ball through the exponential map. The pinching estimates guarantee these two balls already cover the whole manifold, leaving no uncovered region between them.

label: Gluing to a Sphere
notes: The manifold is now two disks overlapping in a collar near their common boundary sphere. Any manifold that is a union of two embedded disks is homeomorphic to the standard sphere, by reversing the equatorial gluing that builds the sphere from two hemispheres. This is the topological punchline of the construction.

label: Sharpness and Rigidity
notes: Quarter pinching is sharp: the complex and quaternionic projective spaces carry metrics with curvature exactly between one quarter and one, but they are not spheres. They show why the inequality at one quarter must be strict. The rigidity case at equality leads to the rich theory of rank one symmetric spaces.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We recapped the logical chain: pinching, Rauch and conjugate points, Klingenberg's injectivity estimate, Bonnet Myers diameter, Toponogov comparison, and the two ball covering that yields a homeomorphism to the sphere. The differentiable sphere theorem and Ricci flow proofs extend this story far beyond our pages.
